summary:
ASTRA V2 is an offline-first Astronaut Health Monitoring and Decision-Support System developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

It provides real-time simulated crew health monitoring, individual astronaut profiles, physiological alerts, medical history, interactive 3D anatomical visualisation, symptom reporting, and ASTRA Assist for offline medical knowledge support.

The platform also includes offline voice input and read-aloud assistance, helping astronauts access health information and interact with the system without relying on an internet connection.
details:
ASTRA V2 – Astronaut Health Monitoring and Decision-Support System

Project Overview

ASTRA V2 is an offline-first Astronaut Health Monitoring and Decision-Support System designed to support astronaut health and crew autonomy during long-duration space missions. Space missions present unique health challenges, including limited access to medical facilities, communication delays with Earth, exposure to radiation, and the physical and physiological effects of living in microgravity.

ASTRA aims to address these challenges by providing a centralised platform where crew health information can be monitored, reviewed, and accessed even when an internet connection is unavailable.

What Does ASTRA Do and How Does It Work?

ASTRA provides a dashboard containing individual profiles for five astronauts. It displays simulated physiological readings, including heart rate, oxygen saturation, breathing rate, and skin temperature. The system monitors incoming readings and highlights potential abnormalities through a health alert system.

Each astronaut has an individual medical profile containing health reports, medical history, and recorded health events. An interactive 3D anatomical model allows users to explore different body regions and view relevant health information.

ASTRA also includes ASTRA Assist, an offline knowledge-support feature that retrieves relevant information from a locally stored knowledge base. Crew members can ask health-related questions and receive structured information, including explanations, warning signs, escalation guidance, and general recommendations.

To improve accessibility and hands-free interaction, ASTRA incorporates offline voice recognition and read-aloud functionality. Crew members can speak questions to the system, receive transcribed input, and choose to have responses read aloud.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRA is designed to:

  • Support continuous crew health monitoring and improve visibility of individual astronaut health status.
  • Help identify potentially concerning physiological changes through alerts.
  • Maintain accessible medical histories and health records.
  • Provide locally available health knowledge without depending on continuous internet connectivity.
  • Support crew autonomy when communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable.
  • Improve accessibility through voice input and spoken responses.

The intended impact is to contribute towards safer and more autonomous human space exploration by giving astronauts better access to their health information and decision-support resources during missions.

Technologies and Tools Used

ASTRA V2 was developed using a combination of web technologies and locally running software.

  • HTML5 – Structure of the application.
  • CSS3 – Interface styling and responsive layout.
  • JavaScript – Frontend functionality, dashboard interactions, data processing, and communication with the backend.
  • Node.js – Backend runtime environment.
  • Express.js – REST API development and communication between application components.
  • SQLite – Local database for crew profiles, readings, alerts, and health records.
  • Python – Offline speech recognition integration.
  • Vosk – Local speech-to-text processing.
  • Three.js – Interactive 3D anatomical visualisation.
  • Fuse.js – Search and retrieval within the local knowledge base.
  • VS Code – Development environment.
  • Git and GitHub – Source-code management and collaboration.

The system uses simulated physiological readings for its prototype demonstration. Its architecture is designed around local processing and data storage to minimise reliance on internet connectivity.

What Makes ASTRA Creative?

ASTRA combines several capabilities into one astronaut-focused platform rather than treating health monitoring, medical records, anatomical visualisation, and knowledge support as separate tools.

Its creative elements include an interactive 3D anatomical model connected to crew health information, offline knowledge retrieval through ASTRA Assist, and integrated offline voice interaction. Combining these features creates a more accessible and interactive health-support environment for astronauts.

The focus on offline functionality is particularly important because future space missions may experience communication delays, limited connectivity, or temporary loss of contact with Earth.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered the unique operational challenges of space exploration, including:

  • Communication limitations: The system should remain useful without a continuous connection to Earth.
  • Crew autonomy: Astronauts should be able to access relevant health information independently.
  • Data accessibility: Health information should be organised into clear profiles, histories, and alerts.
  • Usability: The interface should make important information easy to identify and access.
  • Accessibility: Voice recognition and read-aloud features provide alternative ways to interact with the platform.
  • Data reliability: Simulated readings and system-generated alerts should be clearly distinguished from real medical measurements and diagnoses.
  • Scalability: The platform should allow additional health metrics, knowledge resources, and monitoring capabilities to be introduced in the future.

Conclusion

ASTRA V2 explores how offline-first software, health monitoring, interactive visualisation, and locally accessible knowledge can support astronaut autonomy. By bringing these capabilities together, the project aims to demonstrate how technology can help crews monitor their health, access relevant information, and make more informed decisions during long-duration space missions.
